    "original_path": "03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/facts.md", "title": "facts.md", "support_state":
    "supplied", "source_type": "workspace", "available_excerpt": "# Known Facts\n\n-
    Mosaic Relay is acquiring Harbor Pay; close targeted Nov 15 (~10 weeks out).\n-
    Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts into Mosaic Relay''s
    app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account and balance and full access
    to Mosaic''s product set.\n- Plan is no re-verification; Harbor users were already
    KYC''d by Harbor.\n- Harbor holds money transmitter licenses (MTLs) in 38 states;
    Mosaic Relay holds 41; combined footprint is 44 states, opening four new markets.\n-
    Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; Mosaic has pass/fail
    results for everyone but not the underlying documents for users onboarded before
    2023.\n- Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract
    terminates at close; plan is to repoint Harbor''s transaction feed at Mosaic''s
    engine on day 1.\n- Marketing wants a ''Welcome'' campaign with a $50 bonus on
    first transfer, launching close+1.\n- Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a
    handful'' of SARs from the last year at Harbor; nobody has read them yet.\n- Migration
    moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts into Mosaic Relay''s app on
    day 1 post-close, with one unified account and balance.\n- Plan is no re-verification
    of Harbor''s existing KYC; Harbor users were already KYC''d.\n- Harbor''s KYC
    ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; pass/fail results exist for everyone
    but underlying documents are missing for users onboarded before 2023.\n- Harbor''s
    transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract terminates at close;
    plan is to repoint the transaction feed to Mosaic Relay''s engine on day 1.\n-
    Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs from the last year
    at Harbor; none have been read yet.\n- How is the Harbor Pay acquisition structured?
    — Asset purchase (Mosaic buys Harbor''s assets)\n- Does Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP
    program currently permit relying on another institution''s prior KYC without re-verification,
    or is re-verification required? — Not sure / need to check with compliance\n-
    What is known about Harbor''s ~40 open alerts and the SARs from the last year?
    — Nothing reviewed yet — still in diligence\n- For the four new markets opened
    by the combined footprint, does Mosaic Relay plan to operate under Harbor''s existing
    licenses or apply for its own? — Use/assume Harbor''s licenses\n- For the pre-2023
    Harbor users with no underlying KYC documents, what is the plan to satisfy Mosaic
    Relay''s own BSA/AML customer identification and recordkeeping obligations? —
    It is not yet known whether Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP program permits reliance on
    Harbor''s prior KYC; compliance must confirm.\n- Have the ~40 open alerts and
    the handful of SARs from the last year been reviewed, and what did they reveal?
    — The open alerts and SAR history have not been reviewed and remain in diligence.\n-
    For the four new markets opened by the combined license footprint, what is the
    plan for state money transmission licensing or approval before onboarding those
    customers? — Mosaic Relay currently plans to use or assume Harbor''s licenses
    for the four new markets.\n\n## Assumptions\n\n- [Assumption] Mosaic Relay''s
    existing money transmission licenses and Harbor''s MTLs are transferable or can
    be maintained through the acquisition without new state approval\n- [Assumption]
    The KYC pass/fail results are sufficient to satisfy Mosaic Relay''s own BSA/AML
    program obligations without the underlying documents\n- [Assumption] The transaction
    monitoring repoint can be completed and validated before close without a monitoring
    gap\n- [Assumption] Harbor Pay is a licensed money transmitter subject to state
    MTL regimes and federal BSA/AML obligations (not yet confirmed).\n- [Assumption]
    Mosaic Relay is itself a licensed money transmitter in 41 states (per the request).\n-
    [Assumption] The acquisition is structured as an asset or stock purchase, which
    affects whether Harbor''s licenses and SAR/alert obligations transfer (structure
    not yet confirmed).\n", "selected_passages": [{"start": 0, "end": 3962, "text":
    "# Known Facts\n\n- Mosaic Relay is acquiring Harbor Pay; close targeted Nov 15
    (~10 weeks out).\n- Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts
    into Mosaic Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account and balance
    and full access to Mosaic''s product set.\n- Plan is no re-verification; Harbor
    users were already KYC''d by Harbor.\n- Harbor holds money transmitter licenses
    (MTLs) in 38 states; Mosaic Relay holds 41; combined footprint is 44 states, opening
    four new markets.\n- Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024;
    Mosaic has pass/fail results for everyone but not the underlying documents for
    users onboarded before 2023.\n- Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party
    SaaS whose contract terminates at close; plan is to repoint Harbor''s transaction
    feed at Mosaic''s engine on day 1.\n- Marketing wants a ''Welcome'' campaign with
    a $50 bonus on first transfer, launching close+1.\n- Diligence flagged ~40 open
    alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs from the last year at Harbor; nobody has read
    them yet.\n- Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts into
    Mosaic Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account and balance.\n-
    Plan is no re-verification of Harbor''s existing KYC; Harbor users were already
    KYC''d.\n- Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; pass/fail
    results exist for everyone but underlying documents are missing for users onboarded
    before 2023.\n- Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract
    terminates at close; plan is to repoint the transaction feed to Mosaic Relay''s
    engine on day 1.\n- Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs
    from the last year at Harbor; none have been read yet.\n- How is the Harbor Pay
    acquisition structured? — Asset purchase (Mosaic buys Harbor''s assets)\n- Does
    Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP program currently permit relying on another institution''s
    prior KYC without re-verification, or is re-verification required? — Not sure
    / need to check with compliance\n- What is known about Harbor''s ~40 open alerts
    and the SARs from the last year? — Nothing reviewed yet — still in diligence\n-
    For the four new markets opened by the combined footprint, does Mosaic Relay plan
    to operate under Harbor''s existing licenses or apply for its own? — Use/assume
    Harbor''s licenses\n- For the pre-2023 Harbor users with no underlying KYC documents,
    what is the plan to satisfy Mosaic Relay''s own BSA/AML customer identification
    and recordkeeping obligations? — It is not yet known whether Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP
    program permits reliance on Harbor''s prior KYC; compliance must confirm.\n- Have
    the ~40 open alerts and the handful of SARs from the last year been reviewed,
    and what did they reveal? — The open alerts and SAR history have not been reviewed
    and remain in diligence.\n- For the four new markets opened by the combined license
    footprint, what is the plan for state money transmission licensing or approval
    before onboarding those customers? — Mosaic Relay currently plans to use or assume
    Harbor''s licenses for the four new markets.\n\n## Assumptions\n\n- [Assumption]
    Mosaic Relay''s existing money transmission licenses and Harbor''s MTLs are transferable
    or can be maintained through the acquisition without new state approval\n- [Assumption]
    The KYC pass/fail results are sufficient to satisfy Mosaic Relay''s own BSA/AML
    program obligations without the underlying documents\n- [Assumption] The transaction
    monitoring repoint can be completed and validated before close without a monitoring
    gap\n- [Assumption] Harbor Pay is a licensed money transmitter subject to state
    MTL regimes and federal BSA/AML obligations (not yet confirmed).\n- [Assumption]
    Mosaic Relay is itself a licensed money transmitter in 41 states (per the request).\n-
    [Assumption] The acquisition is structured as an asset or stock purchase, which
    affects whether Harbor''s licenses and SAR/alert obligations transfer (structure
    not yet confirmed).\n"}], "content_truncated": false, "source_label": "facts.md"},

    Transmission Modernization Act", "extraction_state": "complete", "selected_passages":
    [{"unit_id": "p000027", "start": 0, "end": 1943, "page_number": 27, "section_label":
    null, "body_hash": "512d4a7a3e1afc61a66c79b53548e6795e9f434d557b21d346fd4662aaafc705",
    "path": "03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/source-library/SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538/dd8e38dc121ab8ed7fe079b02c7e158a/pages/p000027.md",
    "text": "27 \n \n(c) \nThe audited financial statements shall include or be accompanied
    by a \ncertificate of opinion of the independent certified public accountant or
    independent public \naccountant that is satisfactory in form and content to the
    [Commissioner]. If the certificate or \nopinion is qualified, the [Commissioner]
    may order the licensee to take any action as the \n[Commissioner] may find necessary
    to enable the independent or certified public accountant or \nindependent public
    accountant to remove the qualification. \nSection 7.03 Authorized Delegate Reporting.
    \n(a) \nEach licensee shall submit a report of authorized delegates within 45
    days \nof the end of the calendar quarter.20 The [Commissioner] is authorized
    and encouraged to utilize \nNMLS for the submission of the report required by
    this [Section 7.03(a)] provided that such \nfunctionality is consistent with the
    requirements of this [Section 7.03]. \n(b) \nThe authorized delegate report shall
    include, at a minimum, each authorized \ndelegate''s: \n(1) \nCompany legal name;
    \n(2) \nTaxpayer employer identification number; \n(3) \nPrincipal provider identifier;
    \n(4) \nPhysical address; \n(5) \nMailing address; \n(6) \nAny business conducted
    in other states; \n(7) \nAny fictitious or trade name; \n(8) \nContact person
    name, phone number, and email \n(9) \nStart date as licensee’s authorized delegate;
    \n(10) \nEnd date acting as licensee’s authorized delegate, if applicable;  \n(11)
    \n[Court orders pursuant to [Section 8.03];] and \n(12) \nAny other information
    the [Commissioner] reasonably requires with \nrespect to the authorized delegate.
    \nSection 7.04 Reports of Certain Events.21 \n \n20 Commentary: This language
    is designed to implement state use of the NMLS Uniform Authorized Agent Reporting
    \n(UAAR) process. \n21 Commentary: States are encouraged to utilize NMLS to satisfy
    Section 7.04 reporting requirements if NMLS \ndevelops new functionality to prioritize
    reporting of significant events.\n"}], "support_state": "retrieved", "url": "https://www.csbs.org/sites/default/files/2023-02/CSBS%20Money%20Transmission%20Modernization%20Act.pdf",

    may order the licensee to take any action as the \n[Commissioner] may find necessary
    to enable the independent or certified public accountant or \nindependent public
    accountant to remove the qualification. \nSection 7.03 Authorized Delegate Reporting.
    \n(a) \nEach licensee shall submit a report of authorized delegates within 45
    days \nof the end of the calendar quarter.20 The [Commissioner] is authorized
    and encouraged to utilize \nNMLS for the submission of the report required by
    this [Section 7.03(a)] provided that such \nfunctionality is consistent with the

    include, at a minimum, each authorized \ndelegate''s: \n(1) \nCompany legal name;
    \n(2) \nTaxpayer employer identification number; \n(3) \nPrincipal provider identifier;
    \n(4) \nPhysical address; \n(5) \nMailing address; \n(6) \nAny business conducted
    in other states; \n(7) \nAny fictitious or trade name; \n(8) \nContact person

    \nSection 7.04 Reports of Certain Events.21 \n \n20 Commentary: This language
    is designed to implement state use of the NMLS Uniform Authorized Agent Reporting

    Section 7.04 reporting requirements if NMLS \ndevelops new functionality to prioritize
    reporting of significant events.\n"}, {"source_id": "SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538",
    "source_version": "dd8e38dc121ab8ed7fe079b02c7e158a", "title": "[PDF] CSBS Money
    Transmission Modernization Act", "extraction_state": "complete", "selected_passages":
    [{"unit_id": "p000028", "start": 0, "end": 2132, "page_number": 28, "section_label":
    null, "body_hash": "80c098d06593529d6d6335e3b8a4fe8e8db356a8c5d82eb34a2001d27d642973",
    "path": "03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/source-library/SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538/dd8e38dc121ab8ed7fe079b02c7e158a/pages/p000028.md",
    "text": "28 \n \n(a) \nA licensee shall file a report with the [Commissioner]
    within one business \nday after the licensee has reason to know of the occurrence
    of any of the following events: \n(1) \nthe filing of a petition by or against
    the licensee under the \nUnited States Bankruptcy Code, 11 U.S.C. Section 101-110,
    as amended or recodified from \ntime to time, for bankruptcy or reorganization;
    \n(2) \nthe filing of a petition by or against the licensee for \nreceivership,
    the commencement of any other judicial or administrative proceeding for its \ndissolution
    or reorganization, or the making of a general assignment for the benefit of its
    \ncreditors; or \n(3) \nthe commencement of a proceeding to revoke or suspend
    its \nlicense in a state or country in which the licensee engages in business
    or is licensed. \n(b) \nA licensee shall file a report with the [Commissioner]
    within three business \nday after the licensee has reason to know of the occurrence
    of any of the following events: \n(1) \na [charge or] conviction of the licensee
    or of a key individual \nor person in control of the licensee for a felony; or
    \n(2) \na [charge or] conviction of an authorized delegate for a \nfelony. \nSection
    7.05 Bank Secrecy Act Reports. \nA licensee and an authorized delegate shall file
    all reports required by federal currency \nreporting, record keeping, and suspicious
    activity reporting requirements as set forth in the Bank \nSecrecy Act and other
    federal and state laws pertaining to money laundering. The timely filing of \na
    complete and accurate report required under this [Section 7.05] with the appropriate
    federal \nagency is deemed compliant with the requirements of this [Section 7.05].
    \nSection 7.06 Records. \n(a) \nLicensee shall maintain the following records,
    for determining its \ncompliance with this [Act] for at least [three] years: \n(1)
    \na record of each outstanding money transmission obligation \nsold; \n(2) \na
    general ledger posted at least monthly containing all asset, \nliability, capital,
    income, and expense accounts; \n(3) \nbank statements and bank reconciliation
    records; \n(4) \nrecords of outstanding money transmission obligations;\n"}],

    "text": "29 \n \n(5) \nrecords of each outstanding money transmission obligation
    \npaid within the [three]-year period; \n(6) \na list of the last known names
    and addresses of all of the \nlicensee''s authorized delegates; and \n(7) \nany
    other records the [Commissioner] reasonably requires \nby rule. \n(b) \nThe items
    specified in [Section 7.06(a)] may be maintained in any form of \nrecord. \n(c)
    \nRecords specified in [Section 7.06(a)] may be maintained outside this state
    \nif they are made accessible to the [Commissioner] on [seven] business-days''
    notice that is sent in \na record. \n(d) \nAll records maintained by the licensee
    as required in [Section 7.06(a)–(c)] \nare open to inspection by the [Commissioner]
    pursuant to [Section 4.03(a)]. \n \nARTICLE VIII \nAuthorized Delegates \nSection
    8.01 Relationship Between Licensee and Authorized Delegate. \n(a) \nIn this [Section
    8.01], \"remit\" means to make direct payments of money to \na licensee or its
    representative authorized to receive money or to deposit money in a bank in an
    \naccount specified by the licensee. \n(b) \nBefore a licensee is authorized to
    conduct business through an authorized \ndelegate or allows a person to act as
    the licensee''s authorized delegate, the licensee must: \n(1) \nadopt, and update
    as necessary, written policies and procedures \nreasonably designed to ensure
    that the licensee''s authorized delegates comply with \napplicable state and federal
    law; \n(2) \nenter into a written contract that complies with [Section 8.01(d)];
    \nand \n(3) \nconduct a reasonable risk-based background investigation sufficient
    \nfor the licensee to determine whether the authorized delegate has complied and
    will likely \ncomply with applicable state and federal law. \n(c) \nAn authorized
    delegate must operate in full compliance with this [Act]. \n(d) \nThe written
    contract required by [Section 8.01(b)] must be signed by the \nlicensee and the
    authorized delegate and, at a minimum, must:\n"}], "support_state": "retrieved",

    "source_version": "dd8e38dc121ab8ed7fe079b02c7e158a", "title": "[PDF] CSBS Money
    Transmission Modernization Act", "extraction_state": "complete", "selected_passages":
    [{"unit_id": "p000012", "start": 0, "end": 2795, "page_number": 12, "section_label":
    null, "body_hash": "eb065076e15fd657d0f7643c2decce3eaf1414613758d251ef629d3eaa6ad5c4",
    "path": "03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/source-library/SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538/dd8e38dc121ab8ed7fe079b02c7e158a/pages/p000012.md",
    "text": "12 \n \n(4) \nThe terms of or a copy of any bond filed by a licensee,
    provided that \nconfidential information, including, but not limited to, prices
    and fees for such bond is \nredacted; \n(5) \nCopies of any non-confidential final
    orders of the [Department] \nrelating to any violation of this [Act] or regulations
    implementing this [Act]; and \n(e) \nImposition of an administrative fine or penalty
    under this [Act]. \nSection 4.03 Supervision. \n(a) \nThe [Commissioner] may conduct
    an examination or investigation of a \nlicensee or authorized delegate or otherwise
    take independent action authorized by this [Act] or by \na rule adopted or order
    issued under this [Act] as reasonably necessary or appropriate to administer \nand
    enforce this [Act], regulations implementing this [Act], and other applicable
    law, including \nthe Bank Secrecy Act and the USA PATRIOT ACT.  The [Commissioner]
    may: \n(1) \nconduct an examination either on-site or off-site as the \n[Commissioner]
    may reasonably require; \n(2) \nconduct an examination in conjunction with an
    examination \nconducted by representatives of other state agencies or agencies
    of another state or of the \nfederal government; \n(3) \n  accept the examination
    report of another state agency or an agency \nof another state or of the federal
    government, or a report prepared by an independent \naccounting firm, which on
    being accepted is considered for all purposes as an official report \nof the [Commissioner];
    and \n(4) \nsummon and examine under oath a key individual or employee of a \nlicensee
    or authorized delegate and require the person to produce records regarding any
    \nmatter related to the condition and business of the licensee or authorized delegate.

      path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8
    request_text: '# Original Request


      From: Dana, PM — Growth & Integration

      Subject: Harbor migration — anything here need legal?


      We''re acquiring Harbor Pay. Close is targeted Nov 15 (~10 weeks). Migration
      plan:


      240k consumer users, 12k business accounts move into our app on day 1 post-close.
      One unified account, one balance, full access to our product set.

      No re-verification — they were already KYC''d by Harbor.

      Harbor holds MTLs in 38 states, we hold 41. Combined that''s 44 — nice win,
      opens four new markets.

      Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024. We have pass/fail
      results for everyone, but not the underlying documents for users onboarded before
      2023.

      Harbor''s monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract terminates at close.
      Plan is to repoint their transaction feed at our engine on day 1.

      Marketing wants a "Welcome" campaign with a $50 bonus on first transfer, launching
      close+1.

      Diligence flagged that Harbor has ~40 open alerts and "a handful" of SARs from
      the last year. Nobody''s read them yet.


      Does any of this need legal before close? It''s really just a data migration.

      '
    recommendation:
      matter_id: MAT-20260909-d89ad8
      path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/recommendations.md
      content: '## Working position


        The Harbor Pay migration needs legal and compliance review before the planned
        close. The leading concern is that an asset purchase generally requires Mosaic
        Relay to confirm its own authority to operate in each state; the current plan
        to use or assume Harbor''s licenses is not established as legally effective.


        The second concern is BSA/AML readiness. Mosaic Relay has not confirmed whether
        its AML/CIP program permits reliance on Harbor''s prior KYC, and underlying
        records are missing for some pre-2023 users. Harbor''s open alerts and SAR
        history also remain unread. These gaps make a day-one migration without re-verification
        or account restrictions difficult to support.


        Transaction monitoring continuity is also material because Harbor''s vendor
        ends at close. The repointed feed should be tested and validated before migrated
        users receive full access. The $50 bonus is lower priority but still needs
        review once its eligibility, funding, terms, and disclosures are known.


        ## Plausible alternatives


        A narrower launch could exclude the four new markets, restrict users whose
        KYC evidence is incomplete, or delay full product access until alert review
        and monitoring validation finish. A full day-one launch remains possible only
        if state licensing, AML/CIP reliance, alert handling, and monitoring continuity
        are confirmed.


        ## Material facts and assumptions


        Reported facts include the asset-purchase structure, the current plan to rely
        on Harbor''s licenses, the lack of a compliance answer on KYC reliance, and
        the unread alerts and SAR history. The analysis assumes both entities conduct
        regulated money-transmission activity and that Mosaic Relay will become the
        operating provider immediately after close. It does not assume that Harbor''s
        licenses transfer or that Harbor''s KYC is sufficient.


        ## What could change this view


        The view could change if state counsel confirms an effective licensing path
        for each affected state, compliance confirms permissible reliance with adequate
        records or remediation, diligence clears the alerts and SAR history, and testing
        shows no monitoring gap. The bonus structure remains unknown.


        ## Support limit


        This is generated analysis based on reported matter facts. No external authority
        was retrieved.'

          underlying records are missing for some pre-2023 users. Harbor''s open alerts
          and SAR history also remain unread. These gaps make a day-one migration
          without re-verification or account restrictions difficult to support.


          Transaction monitoring continuity is also material because Harbor''s vendor
          ends at close. The repointed feed should be tested and validated before

          <details>

          <summary>Earlier saved position — 2026-09-09T20:57:53+00:00</summary>


          **Working position**


          The Harbor Pay migration needs legal and compliance review before the planned
          close. The leading concern is that an asset purchase generally requires
          Mosaic Relay to confirm its own authority to operate in each state; the
          current plan to use or assume Harbor''s licenses is not established as legally
          effective.


          The second concern is BSA/AML readiness. Mosaic Relay has not confirmed
          whether its AML/CIP program permits reliance on Harbor''s prior KYC, and
          underlying records are missing for some pre-2023 users. Harbor''s open alerts
          and SAR history also remain unread. These gaps make a day-one migration
          without re-verification or account restrictions difficult to support.


          Transaction monitoring continuity is also material because Harbor''s vendor
          ends at close. The repointed feed should be tested and validated before
          migrated users receive full access. The $50 bonus is lower priority but
          still needs review once its eligibility, funding, terms, and disclosures
          are known.


          **Plausible alternatives**


          A narrower launch could exclude the four new markets, restrict users whose
          KYC evidence is incomplete, or delay full product access until alert review
          and monitoring validation finish. A full day-one launch remains possible
          only if state licensing, AML/CIP reliance, alert handling, and monitoring
          continuity are confirmed.


          **Material facts and assumptions**


          Reported facts include the asset-purchase structure, the current plan to
          rely on Harbor''s licenses, the lack of a compliance answer on KYC reliance,
          and the unread alerts and SAR history. The analysis assumes both entities
          conduct regulated money-transmission activity and that Mosaic Relay will
          become the operating provider immediately after close. It does not assume
          that Harbor''s licenses transfer or that Harbor''s KYC is sufficient.


          **What could change this view**


          The view could change if state counsel confirms an effective licensing path
          for each affected state, compliance confirms permissible reliance with adequate
          records or remediation, diligence clears the alerts and SAR history, and
          testing shows no monitoring gap. The bonus structure remains unknown.


          **Support limit**


          This is generated analysis based on reported matter facts. No external authority
          was retrieved.


          </details>'

                  text: "14 \n \nARTICLE V \nMoney Transmission Licenses \nSection
                    5.01 License Required. \n(a) \nA person may not engage in the
                    business of money transmission or \nadvertise, solicit, or hold
                    itself out as providing money transmission unless the person is
                    licensed \nunder this [Act]; \n(b) \n[Section 5.01(a)] does not
                    apply to: \n(1) \nA person that is an authorized delegate of a
                    person licensed under \nthis [Act] acting within the scope of
                    authority conferred by a written contract with the \nlicensee;
                    or \n(2) \nA person that is exempt pursuant to [Section 3.01]
                    and does not \nengage in money transmission outside the scope
                    of such exemption. \n(c) \nA license issued under [Section 5.05]
                    is not transferable or assignable. \nSection 5.02 Consistent State
                    Licensing. \n(a) \nTo establish consistent licensing between [this
                    state] and other states, the \n[Commissioner] is authorized and
                    encouraged to: \n(1) \nimplement all licensing provisions of this
                    [Act] in a manner that is \nconsistent with other states that
                    have adopted this [Act]or multistate licensing processes; \nand
                    \n(2) \nparticipate in nationwide protocols for licensing cooperation
                    and \ncoordination among state regulators provided that such protocols
                    are consistent with this \n[Act]. \n(b) \nIn order to fulfill
                    the purposes of this [Act], the [Commissioner] is \nauthorized
                    and encouraged to establish relationships or contracts with NMLS
                    or other entities \ndesignated by NMLS to enable the [Commissioner]
                    to: \n(1) \ncollect and maintain records; \n(2) \ncoordinate multistate
                    licensing processes and supervision processes; \n(3) \nprocess
                    fees; and \n(4) \nfacilitate communication between [state] and
                    licensees or other \npersons subject to this [Act]. \n(c) \nThe
                    [Commissioner] is authorized and encouraged to utilize NMLS for
                    all \naspects of licensing in accordance with this [Act], including
                    but not limited to, license applications, \napplications for acquisitions
                    of control, surety bonds, reporting, criminal history background\n"

                  text: "22 \n \n(e) \nWhen an application for acquisition of control

                    address all of the matters that are required, the application
                    shall \nbe considered complete and the [Commissioner] shall promptly
                    notify the applicant in a record of \nthe date on which the application
                    was determined to be complete and:15 \n \n(1) \nThe [Commissioner]
                    shall approve or deny the application within 60 \ndays after the
                    completion date; or \n(2) \nif the application is not approved
                    or denied within 60 days after the \ncompletion date: \n(A) \nthe
                    application is approved; and \n(B) \nthe person, or group of persons
                    acting in concert, are not \nprohibited from acquiring control.
                    \n(3) \nThe [Commissioner] may for good cause extend the application
                    \nperiod. \n(f) \nA determination by the [Commissioner] that an
                    application is complete and \nis accepted for processing means
                    only that the application, on its face, appears to include all
                    of the \nitems and address all of the matters that are required,
                    and is not an assessment of the substance of \nthe application
                    or of the sufficiency of the information provided. \n(g) \nWhen
                    an application is filed and considered complete under [Section
                    \n6.01(e)], the [Commissioner] shall investigate the financial
                    condition and responsibility, financial \nand business experience,
                    character, and general fitness of the person, or group of persons
                    acting in \nconcert, seeking to acquire control. The [Commissioner]
                    shall approve an acquisition of control \npursuant to this [Section
                    6.01] if the [Commissioner] finds that all of the following conditions
                    have \nbeen fulfilled: \n(1) \nThe requirements of subsections
                    (b) and (d) have been met, as \napplicable; and \n(2) \nthe financial
                    condition and responsibility, financial and business \nexperience,
                    competence, character, and general fitness of the person, or group
                    of persons \nacting in concert, seeking to acquire control; and
                    the competence, experience, character, \nand general fitness of
                    the key individuals and persons that would be in control of the
                    \nlicensee after the acquisition of control indicate that it is
                    in the interest of the public to \npermit the person, or group
                    of persons acting in concert, to control the licensee. \n(h) \nIf
                    an applicant avails itself or is otherwise subject to a multistate
                    licensing \n \n15 Commentary: NMLS will accommodate and streamline
                    the process of communicating when applications are \nreceived
                    and when states consider them to have been complete. The intent
                    of this Act is for the application period to \nbegin on the day
                    an application is determined to be complete.\n"

              - source_id: SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538
                source_version: dd8e38dc121ab8ed7fe079b02c7e158a
                title: '[PDF] CSBS Money Transmission Modernization Act'
                extraction_state: complete
                selected_passages:
                - unit_id: p000023
                  start: 0
                  end: 2523
                  page_number: 23
                  section_label: null
                  body_hash: 83a664c778fbc9de0b4d13270e2a918f6488b461db1a6617e3d36032163068ca
                  path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/source-library/SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538/dd8e38dc121ab8ed7fe079b02c7e158a/pages/p000023.md
                  text: "23 \n \nprocess: \n(1) \nthe [Commissioner] is authorized
                    and encouraged to accept the \ninvestigation results of a lead
                    investigative state for the purpose of [Section 6.01(g)] if the
                    \nlead investigative state has sufficient staffing, expertise,
                    and minimum standards; or \n(2) \nif [state] is a lead investigative
                    state, the [Commissioner] is \nauthorized and encouraged to investigate
                    the applicant pursuant to [Section 6.01(g)] and \nthe timeframes
                    established by agreement through the multistate licensing process.
                    \n(i) \nThe [Commissioner] shall issue a formal written notice
                    of the denial of an \napplication to acquire control within thirty
                    (30) days of the decision to deny the application. The \n[Commissioner]
                    shall set forth in the notice of denial the specific reasons for
                    the denial of the \napplication. An applicant whose application
                    is denied by the [Commissioner] under this [Section \n6.01(i)]
                    may appeal within thirty (30) days16 after receipt of the written
                    notice of the denial \n[pursuant to state administrative law procedures].
                    \n(j) \nThe requirements of [Section 6.01(a) and (b)] do not apply
                    to any of the \nfollowing: \n(1) \nA person that acts as a proxy
                    for the sole purpose of voting at a \ndesignated meeting of the
                    shareholders or holders of voting shares or voting interests of
                    a \nlicensee or a person in control of a licensee; \n(2) \nA person
                    that acquires control of a licensee by devise or descent; \n(3)
                    \nA person that acquires control of a licensee as a personal \nrepresentative,
                    custodian, guardian, conservator, or trustee, or as an officer
                    appointed by a \ncourt of competent jurisdiction or by operation
                    of law; \n(4) \nA person that is exempt under [Section 3.01(g)];
                    \n(5) \nA person that the [Commissioner] determines is not subject
                    to \n[Section 6.01(a)] based on the public interest; \n(6) \nA
                    public offering of securities of a licensee or a person in control
                    of \na licensee; or \n(7) \nAn internal reorganization of a person
                    in control of the licensee \nwhere the ultimate person in control
                    of the licensee remains the same. \n(k) \nPersons in [Sections
                    6.01(j)(2), (3), (4), (6), (7)] in cooperation with the \nlicensee
                    shall notify the [Commissioner] within [15] days after the acquisition
                    of control.17 \n \n16 Commentary: Administrative procedures for
                    challenging a departmental decision may be derived from other
                    \naspects of state law. In such a case, this Act should be adjusted
                    to reflect the relevant administrative process. \n17 Commentary:
                    Notice is satisfied upon updating the licensee’s NMLS record.\n"

                  shareholders or holders of voting shares or voting interests of
                  a \nlicensee or a person in control of a licensee; \n(2) \nA person
                  that acquires control of a licensee by devise or descent; \n(3)

                  custodian, guardian, conservator, or trustee, or as an officer appointed

                  \nA person that is exempt under [Section 3.01(g)]; \n(5) \nA person
                  that the [Commissioner] determines is not subject to \n[Section
                  6.01(a)] based on the public interest; \n(6) \nA public offering
                  of securities of a licensee or a person in control of \na licensee;
                  or \n(7) \nAn internal reorganization of a person in control of
                  the licensee \nwhere the ultimate person in control of the licensee

                  body_hash: 4732d9c2b053975a4d3cb27db8e99faa4baf45f71eb350fa519e31b5890ac680
                  path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/source-library/SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538/dd8e38dc121ab8ed7fe079b02c7e158a/pages/p000024.md
                  text: "24 \n \n(l) \nStreamlined Acquisition of Control \n(1) \nThe
                    requirements of [Section 6.01(a) and (b)] do not apply to a \nperson
                    that has complied with and received approval to engage in money
                    transmission \nunder this [Act] or was identified as a person
                    in control in a prior application filed with and \napproved by
                    the [Commissioner] or by an MSB accredited state pursuant to a
                    multistate \nlicensing process, provided that: \n(A) \nthe person
                    has not had a license revoked or suspended or \ncontrolled a licensee
                    that has had a license revoked or suspended while the person \nwas
                    in control of the licensee in the previous 5-years; \n(B) \nif
                    the person is a licensee, the person is well managed and \nhas
                    received at least a satisfactory rating for compliance at its
                    most recent \nexamination by an MSB accredited state if such rating
                    was given; \n(C) \nthe licensee to be acquired is projected to
                    meet the \nrequirements of [Sections 10.01, 10.02, and 10.03]
                    of this [Act] after the acquisition \nof control is completed,
                    and if the person acquiring control is a licensee, that \nlicensee
                    is also projected to meet the requirements of [Sections 10.01,
                    10.02, and \n10.03] of this [Act] after the acquisition of control
                    is completed; \n(D) \nthe licensee to be acquired will not implement
                    any material \nchanges to its business plan as a result of the
                    acquisition of control, and if the person \nacquiring control
                    is a licensee, that licensee also will not implement any material
                    \nchanges to its business plan as a result of the acquisition
                    of control;  and \n(E) \nthe person provides notice of the acquisition
                    in cooperation \nwith the licensee and attests to [Section 6.01(l)(1)(A),
                    (B), (C), and (D)] in a form \nand in a medium prescribed by the
                    [Commissioner]. \n(2) \nIf the notice is not disapproved within
                    30 days after the date on \nwhich the notice was determined to
                    be complete, the notice is deemed approved. \n(m) \nBefore filing
                    an application for approval to acquire control of a licensee a
                    \nperson may request in writing a determination from the [Commissioner]
                    as to whether the person \nwould be considered a person in control
                    of a licensee upon consummation of a proposed \ntransaction. If
                    the [Commissioner] determines that the person would not be a person
                    in control of \na licensee, the proposed Person and transaction
                    is not subject to the requirements of [Section \n6.01(a) and (b)]
                    of this [Act]. \n(n) \nIf a multistate licensing process includes
                    a determination pursuant to \n[Section 6.01(m)] and an applicant
                    avails itself or is otherwise subject to the multistate licensing
                    \nprocess: \n(1) \nThe [Commissioner] is authorized and encouraged
                    to accept the \ncontrol determination of a lead investigative
                    state with sufficient staffing, expertise, and \nminimum standards
                    for the purpose of [Section 6.01(m)]; or\n"

                  body_hash: 2245b178c49fc1f157bf15c133c59f8fcfe9abdf43f0bf94df397229a7889584
                  path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/source-library/SRC-37ee676da5b354ba8538/dd8e38dc121ab8ed7fe079b02c7e158a/pages/p000004.md
                  text: "ly for goods or services provided by the issuer or its affiliate
                    or franchisees of the issuer \nor its affiliate, except to the
                    extent required by applicable law to be redeemable in cash for
                    its cash \nvalue; \n(f) \n\"Control\" means \n(1) \n(A) the power
                    to vote, directly or indirectly, at least 25 percent of \nthe
                    outstanding voting shares or voting interests of a licensee or
                    person in control of a \nlicensee; \n(B) \nthe power to elect
                    or appoint a majority of key individuals or \nexecutive officers,
                    managers, directors, trustees, or other persons exercising \nmanagerial
                    authority of a person in control of a licensee; or \n(C) \nthe
                    power to exercise, directly or indirectly, a controlling \ninfluence
                    over the management or policies of a licensee or person in control
                    of a \nlicensee. \n(2) \nRebuttable Presumption of Control. \n(A)
                    \nA person is presumed to exercise a controlling influence \nwhen
                    the person holds the power to vote, directly or indirectly, at
                    least 10 percent \nof the outstanding voting shares or voting
                    interests of a licensee or person in control \nof a licensee.2
                    \n(B) \nA person presumed to exercise a controlling influence
                    as \ndefined by this [Section 2.01(f)] can rebut the presumption
                    of control if the person \nis a passive investor. \n(3) \nFor
                    purposes of determining the percentage of a person controlled
                    \nby any other person, the person's interest shall be aggregated
                    with the interest of any other \nimmediate family member, including
                    the person's spouse, parents, children, siblings, \nmothers- and
                    fathers-in law, sons- and daughters-in-law, brothers- and sisters-in-law,
                    and \nany other person who shares such person's home. \n(g) \n\"Eligible
                    rating\" shall mean a credit rating of any of the three highest
                    rating \ncategories provided by an eligible rating service, whereby
                    each category may include rating \n \n2 Commentary: The obligation
                    to rebut control rests exclusively with the person acquiring ≥10%
                    of the outstanding \nvoting shares or voting interests of a licensee
                    or person in control of a licensee.  It is not the responsibility
                    of the \nlicensee to rebut control.  This is consistent with Section
                    601(a) of the Act which requires the person acquiring control
                    \nto obtain prior approval.\n"

                  text: "30 \n \n(1) \nappoint the person signing the contract as

                  text: "31 \n \nfees received from money transmission.22 \n(g) \nAn
                    authorized delegate may not use a subdelegate to conduct money
                    \ntransmission on behalf of a licensee. \nSection 8.02 Unauthorized
                    Activities \nA person shall not engage in the business of money
                    transmission on behalf of a person \nnot licensed under this [Act]
                    \ or not exempt pursuant to [Article III] of this [Act]. A person
                    that \nengages in such activity provides money transmission to
                    the same extent as if the person were a \nlicensee, and shall
                    be jointly and severally liable with the unlicensed or nonexempt
                    person. \nSection 8.03 [Optional]: Prohibited Authorized Delegates.
                    \n(a) \nThe [appropriate court] in an action brought by a licensee
                    shall have \njurisdiction to grant appropriate equitable or legal
                    relief, including without limitation prohibiting \nthe authorized
                    delegate from directly or indirectly acting as an authorized delegate
                    for any licensee \nin this state and the payment of restitution,
                    damages or other monetary relief, if the [appropriate \ncourt]
                    finds that an authorized delegate failed to remit money in accordance
                    with the written \ncontract required by [Section 8.01(b)] or as
                    otherwise directed by the licensee or required by law. \n(b) \nIf
                    the [appropriate court] issues an order prohibiting a person from
                    acting as \nan authorized delegate for any licensee pursuant to
                    [Section 8.03(a)], the licensee that brought the \naction shall
                    report the order to the [Commissioner] within thirty (30) days
                    and shall report the \norder through NMLS within ninety (90) days.
                    \n(c) \nAn authorized delegate who holds money in trust for the
                    benefit of a \nlicensee and knowingly fails to remit more than
                    [$XXX] of such money is guilty of a [reference \nto state classification]
                    felony. \n(d) \nAn authorized delegate who holds money in trust
                    for the benefit of a \nlicensee and knowingly fails to remit no
                    more than [$XXX] of such money is guilty of a [reference \nto
                    state classification] misdemeanor. \nARTICLE IX  \nTimely Transmission,
                    Refunds, and Disclosures \nSection 9.01 Timely Transmission. \n(a)
                    \nEvery licensee shall forward all money received for transmission
                    in \naccordance with the terms of the agreement between the licensee
                    and the sender unless the licensee \nhas a reasonable belief or
                    a reasonable basis to believe that the sender may be a victim
                    of fraud or \nthat a crime or violation of law, rule, or regulation
                    has occurred, is occurring, or may occur. \n(b) \nIf a licensee
                    fails to forward money received for transmission in accordance
                    \nwith this section, the licensee must respond to inquiries by
                    the sender with the reason for the failure \n \n22 Commentary:
                    An express trust account or segregated bank account is not required.\n"

                  body_hash: 3c6e0983ad889dc93334add58721659be3ac3d4bf1075f544bcd9c940396e471
                  path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/source-library/SRC-71b20ecf65825d6522c4/d021ece0cde82565eb83511c8122c85b/sections/s000001.md
                  text: 'ey Transmitter License.


                    Access to NMLS


                    NMLS is a secure web-based system created by state regulators
                    to provide efficiencies in the processing of state licenses and
                    improve supervision of state-regulated industries.


                    To access NMLS for the first time, you must complete a Company
                    Account Request Form and identify a Primary Account Administrator
                    and a Secondary Account Administrator. This form can be submitted
                    online through the NMLS website in the Getting Started section.
                    This form needs to be submitted only once per company, regardless
                    of the number of NMLS participating states in which you are licensed.


                    Within three days of completing and submitting the Company Account
                    Request Form, the Primary Account Administrator will receive NMLS
                    login information. The Primary Account Administrator will have
                    full rights to access the system, submit information to this agency
                    and other participating state regulators, and set up other company
                    users in the system. Instructions and tutorials on how to access
                    and use the system are also available in the NMLS Resource Center
                    .


                    Note : If your company already has a record in NMLS, you can omit
                    this step.


                    Managing Your License on NMLS


                    Each company holding a DFS Money Transmitter License who wishes
                    to manage their license on NMLS must create a company record in
                    the system. To gain access to NMLS, the applicant must submit
                    a form requesting an NMLS account.


                    Current New York State Money Transmitters may transition their
                    licenses to NMLS. See the DFS Money Transmitter Transition Checklist
                    for more information.


                    Submitting a Complete Application


                    To submit an application and ensure your application is received,
                    acknowledged as complete, and processed, please follow the instructions
                    on the DFS Money Transmitter Checklists . No application shall
                    be deemed to be complete until the Department has received all
                    required information, documents, and fees.


                    In the process of reviewing and considering the application, DFS
                    may request additional information and supporting documents.


                    In the application process, an NMLS Identification Number will
                    be assigned to your application. Please maintain a record of this
                    NMLS Identification Number, as it will be used as your application
                    reference number throughout the remainder of the application process.
                    The applicant’s NMLS Identification Number must be included on
                    every hard-copy document submitted to the Department.


                    Note : If the applicant has already submitted Forms MU1 and MU2
                    through NMLS for another state, the applicant does not need to
                    re-enter the company record into NMLS. However, the applicant
                    is required to provide jurisdiction-specific information to support
                    its New York State application.


                    Back to Top ▲


                    Next Section


                    Continue


                    Annual Reporting


                    The Annual Report should be prepared by qualified persons and
                    submitted within 120 days following the close of the calendar
                    year January 1 to December 31, 2025.


                    2025 NMLS Money Transmitter Annual Report Form


                    2025 Non-NMLS Money Transmitter Annual Report Form


                    Back to Top ▲


                    Next Section


                    Continue


                    Reporting Change in Certain Individuals


                    Pursuant to the following sections of the New York Banking Law
                    (BL) and Superintendent’s Regulations (SR), licensees of the Department
                    of Financial Services (DFS) are required to notify the Superintendent
                    of changes in certain individuals, within stipulated time frames:


                    Money Transmitters: BL 641, 642 and 652-a; and SR 406.11


                    These requirements are for changes in certain individuals of licensees
                    whose licenses are not managed on NMLS. For those managed on NMLS,
                    visit the NMLS section website for New York State and navigate
                    to Company Licenses and Amendment under the pertinent industry
                    type, and look under Change in Control on the Amendment Checklist.


                    Included Individuals


                    Members of the governing board such as directors, trustees, and
                    LLC members


                    Officers (at a minimum Chief Executive Officer, President, Chief
                    Financial Officer, Chief Compliance Officer, and Chief Operations
                    Officer, and any other officers deemed necessary by DFS)


                    Documentary requirements for Each Included Individual Being Added


                    Notification on the licensee''s letterhead signed by an authorized
                    officer containing the following:


                    Name and title of the individual being added


                    Effective date of the addition


                    Name and title of the person being replaced, and his/her new title/position,
                    if any


                    Resolution of the governing board approving the addition


                    Personal Questionnaire (PDF)


                    Fingerprints


                    Background Investigation Report *


                    Litigation Affidavit (PDF)


                    Authority to Release Information (PDF)


                    Resume


                    Documentary requirements for Each Included Individual Being Removed:


                    Notification on the licensee''s letterhead signed by an authorized
                    officer containing the following:


                    Name and title of the individual being removed


                    Reason of the removal


                    Effective date of the removal


                    New title/position, if any


                    Where To Submit?'

                  path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/source-library/SRC-b48d8d40f5a0cfe9a200/6ebc7b743e605b8e05363eb0628942c1/sections/s000002.md
                  text: 'How To Get A Money Transmitter License (MTL) in the U.S.


                    Published Date  January 29, 2026


                    To get a Money Transmitter License (MTL), businesses must undergo
                    a rigorous application process that involves dual compliance with
                    federal (like FinCEN''s AML/KYC protocols) and varying state-level
                    regulations. Key requirements across states include demonstrating
                    financial viability, often requiring a surety bond and capital
                    reserves, passing comprehensive background checks for key personnel,
                    and establishing a robust internal compliance program. The process
                    is complex, time-consuming, and mandates extensive documentation
                    and financial disclosures to ensure the applicant is law-abiding
                    and financially sound.


                    Operating a money transfer service in the U.S. involves tackling
                    a myriad of federal and state laws, making how to get a money
                    transmitter license both time-consuming and expensive. Compliance
                    with agencies like FinCEN is non-negotiable to prevent illegal
                    activities.


                    Companies can either secure their own MSB license or partner with
                    a licensed entity, but legal adherence is vital in both scenarios.
                    It''s essential to understand what a money transmitter license
                    is and who needs it.


                    What is a Money Transmitter License?


                    A Money Transmitter License is an official authorization or money
                    service business license that empowers a firm or individual to
                    facilitate the movement of capital. This license enables MSBs
                    to handle financial transactions, ranging from digital payments
                    to wire transfers.


                    Possessing a Money Transmitter License brings forth substantial
                    regulatory oversight. Organizations must prove they have the governance
                    structure and internal controls to manage and safeguard client
                    funds. States will continually scrutinize applicants, denying
                    licensure to those who fail to meet the stringent criteria.


                    In the United States, the need for a Money Transmitter License
                    is not a choice; it''s a requirement for virtually any business
                    involved in the handling or transferring of funds. Money transmitter
                    license requirements by state can vary, so it''s crucial to be
                    aware of the respective state money transmitter regulations.


                    How to Get a Money Transmitter License?


                    The license application process is designed to be rigorous, ensuring
                    that approved businesses are law-abiding and financially sound.
                    Federal and state-level regulations diverge, with each state setting
                    its own financial criteria and often requiring a minimum capital
                    commitment.


                    Applicants typically need a surety bond of at least $500,000 per
                    state, with costs influenced by credit history. The duration to
                    obtain the license varies, contingent on the business type and
                    the state of operation.


                    Money Transmitter License Requirements


                    Acquiring a money transmitter license involves compliance with
                    Anti-Money Laundering (AML) and Know Your Customer (KYC) protocols.
                    While these regulations are federal, individual states often impose
                    additional requirements, thereby necessitating dual compliance.


                    Subsequent to application submission, state authorities undertake
                    an investigative review, focusing on financial sustainability
                    and the applicant''s background.


                    Standardized Requirements Across States


                    Registration: Initial registration typically occurs with the Financial
                    Crimes Enforcement Network or a similar state-level body.'

                available_excerpt: 'How To Get A Money Transmitter License (MTL) in
                  the U.S.


                  Published Date  January 29, 2026


                  To get a Money Transmitter License (MTL), businesses must undergo
                  a rigorous application process that involves dual compliance with
                  federal (like FinCEN''s AML/KYC protocols) and varying state-level
                  regulations. Key requirements across states include demonstrating
                  financial viability, often requiring a surety bond and capital reserves,
                  passing comprehensive background checks for key personnel, and establishing
                  a robust internal compliance program. The process is complex, time-consuming,
                  and mandates extensive documentation and financial disclosures to
                  ensure the applicant is law-abiding and financially sound.


                  Operating a money transfer service in the U.S. involves tackling
                  a myriad of federal and state laws, making how to get a money transmitter
                  license both time-consuming and expensive. Compliance with agencies
                  like FinCEN is non-negotiable to prevent illegal activities.


                  Companies can either secure their own MSB license or partner with
                  a licensed entity, but legal adherence is vital in both scenarios.
                  It''s essential to understand what a money transmitter license is
                  and who needs it.


                  What is a Money Transmitter License?


                  A Money Transmitter License is an official authorization or money
                  service business license that empowers a firm or individual to facilitate
                  the movement of capital. This license enables MSBs to handle financial
                  transactions, ranging from digital payments to wire transfers.


                  Possessing a Money Transmitter License brings forth substantial
                  regulatory oversight. Organizations must prove they have the governance
                  structure and internal controls to manage and safeguard client funds.
                  States will continually scrutinize applicants, denying licensure
                  to those who fail to meet the stringent criteria.


                  In the United States, the need for a Money Transmitter License is
                  not a choice; it''s a requirement for virtually any business involved
                  in the handling or transferring of funds. Money transmitter license
                  requirements by state can vary, so it''s crucial to be aware of
                  the respective state money transmitter regulations.


                  How to Get a Money Transmitter License?


                  The license application process is designed to be rigorous, ensuring
                  that approved businesses are law-abiding and financially sound.
                  Federal and state-level regulations diverge, with each state setting
                  its own financial criteria and often requiring a minimum capital
                  commitment.


                  Applicants typically need a surety bond of at least $500,000 per
                  state, with costs influenced by credit history. The duration to
                  obtain the license varies, contingent on the business type and the
                  state of operation.


                  Money Transmitter License Requirements


                  Acquiring a money transmitter license involves compliance with Anti-Money
                  Laundering (AML) and Know Your Customer (KYC) protocols. While these
                  regulations are federal, individual states often impose additional
                  requirements, thereby necessitating dual compliance.


                  Subsequent to application submission, state authorities undertake
                  an investigative review, focusing on financial sustainability and
                  the applicant''s background.


                  Standardized Requirements Across States


                  Registration: Initial registration typically occurs with the Financial
                  Crimes Enforcement Network or a similar state-level body.'

                title: OCC Confirms National Bank Act Preempts State Money Transmitter
                  ...
                extraction_state: complete
                selected_passages:
                - unit_id: s000001
                  start: 600
                  end: 4794
                  page_number: null
                  section_label: Section 1
                  body_hash: 8ef30c0b98621db1f11c16332c16e9928ea8f237d6b055f645f7b449f18cbdfb
                  path: 03_Matters/harbor-2-d89ad8/research/source-library/SRC-e6c1e4e85e004ccbe413/e06621859d4ec9431f2712a7c357b112/sections/s000001.md
                  text: ', 2026


                    Posted in Bank Regulatory


                    On May 12, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC)
                    issued a significant interpretive letter confirming that Fidelity
                    Digital Assets, National Association (the recently converted national
                    trust bank formerly known as Fidelity Digital Assets Service,
                    LLC) is not required to hold state money transmitter licenses
                    to conduct its federally authorized activities. The OCC concluded
                    that the National Bank Act preempts any state money transmitter
                    licensing requirement as applied to a national bank.


                    Until December 12, 2025, Fidelity Digital Assets operated as a
                    New York-chartered limited liability trust company and held money
                    transmitter licenses in numerous states, including Iowa. On that
                    date, the OCC approved its conversion to an uninsured national
                    trust bank under 12 U.S.C. § 27(a). Concurrent with the conversion,
                    the Bank surrendered its Iowa money transmitter license.


                    Iowa pushed back. Its money transmitter statute exempts banks
                    and trust companies from licensing, but only if they hold federally
                    insured deposits. Because Fidelity Digital Assets is an uninsured
                    national bank, Iowa argued the exemption did not apply and requested
                    a legal basis for the license surrender. Fidelity Digital Assets
                    responded that the National Bank Act preempts Iowa’s requirements
                    and asked the OCC to confirm that position.


                    The OCC’s analysis of whether a state can require a national bank
                    to obtain a state money transmitter license as a condition of
                    engaging in federally authorized activities, including cryptocurrency
                    custody, trade execution, stablecoin issuance, and related digital
                    asset services, rested on two independent and well-established
                    pillars of federal banking law:


                    1. National Bank Act Preemption


                    Federal law authorizes national banks to conduct a broad range
                    of activities on a national basis. Any state law that “prevents
                    or significantly interferes” with a national bank’s exercise of
                    its federally authorized powers is preempted.


                    The OCC reasoned that requiring a national bank to obtain a state
                    money transmitter license, even as a threshold condition to operating,
                    would impermissibly condition the Bank’s federal authority on
                    state approval. At the extreme, a state could veto federal authority
                    outright by denying or revoking a license. Both outcomes are squarely
                    preempted. This conclusion applies to any state’s money transmitter
                    licensing regime, including states that limit their licensing
                    exemptions to a subset of national banks (such as Iowa’s insured-deposits-only
                    carveout).


                    2. Exclusive Federal Visitorial Authority


                    Separately, 12 U.S.C. § 484 vests the OCC with exclusive visitorial
                    authority over national banks. “No national bank shall be subject
                    to any visitorial powers except as authorized by Federal law.”
                    Iowa’s money transmitter statute grants the state agency robust
                    supervisory jurisdiction over licensees, including the power to
                    demand books and records, conduct periodic examinations, take
                    enforcement actions, and even place a licensee into receivership.
                    Applying that regime to a national bank would be “fundamentally
                    inconsistent” with the OCC’s exclusive visitorial powers and is
                    therefore impermissible on independent grounds.


                    Together, these two bases lead to a clean and sweeping conclusion:
                    a national bank may conduct its federally authorized activities
                    in any state without a state money transmitter license, regardless
                    of whether it qualifies for any state-law exemption.


                    Our Take


                    The OCC’s conclusion here was entirely expected. The preemption
                    framework for national banks is well-settled, and the OCC’s letter
                    largely restates principles the Supreme Court and federal courts
                    have applied for decades. That said, one nuance in this letter
                    deserves closer attention: state-chartered trust banks are in
                    a very different position.


                    Unlike national banks, state trust companies and state-chartered
                    banks do not benefit from National Bank Act preemption. Their
                    ability to avoid state money transmitter licensing requirements
                    depends entirely on how each individual state defines “bank” or
                    “trust company” in its money transmission statute and those definitions
                    vary considerably.

                  its federally authorized activities. The OCC concluded that the
                  National Bank Act preempts any state money transmitter licensing
                  requirement as applied to a national bank.


                  Until December 12, 2025, Fidelity Digital Assets operated as a New

                  approved its conversion to an uninsured national trust bank under

                  its Iowa money transmitter license.

                  and asked the OCC to confirm that position.

                  in federally authorized activities, including cryptocurrency custody,
                  trade execution, stablecoin issuance, and related digital asset
                  services, rested on two independent and well-established pillars
                  of federal banking law:


                  1. National Bank Act Preemption

                  The OCC reasoned that requiring a national bank to obtain a state
                  money transmitter license, even as a threshold condition to operating,
                  would impermissibly condition the Bank’s federal authority on state

                  by denying or revoking a license. Both outcomes are squarely preempted.

                  regime, including states that limit their licensing exemptions to
                  a subset of national banks (such as Iowa’s insured-deposits-only
                  carveout).


                  2. Exclusive Federal Visitorial Authority


                  Separately, 12 U.S.C. § 484 vests the OCC with exclusive visitorial

                  to any visitorial powers except as authorized by Federal law.” Iowa’s

                  and records, conduct periodic examinations, take enforcement actions,

                  Together, these two bases lead to a clean and sweeping conclusion:
                  a national bank may conduct its federally authorized activities
                  in any state without a state money transmitter license, regardless

                  Our Take


                  The OCC’s conclusion here was entirely expected. The preemption
                  framework for national banks is well-settled, and the OCC’s letter
                  largely restates principles the Supreme Court and federal courts
                  have applied for decades. That said, one nuance in this letter deserves
                  closer attention: state-chartered trust banks are in a very different
                  position.


                  Unlike national banks, state trust companies and state-chartered
                  banks do not benefit from National Bank Act preemption. Their ability
                  to avoid state money transmitter licensing requirements depends
                  entirely on how each individual state defines “bank” or “trust company”
                  in its money transmission statute and those definitions vary considerably.

                title: facts.md
                support_state: supplied
                source_type: workspace
                available_excerpt: '# Known Facts


                  - Mosaic Relay is acquiring Harbor Pay; close targeted Nov 15 (~10
                  weeks out).

                  - Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts
                  into Mosaic Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account
                  and balance and full access to Mosaic''s product set.

                  - Plan is no re-verification; Harbor users were already KYC''d by
                  Harbor.

                  - Harbor holds money transmitter licenses (MTLs) in 38 states; Mosaic
                  Relay holds 41; combined footprint is 44 states, opening four new
                  markets.

                  - Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; Mosaic
                  has pass/fail results for everyone but not the underlying documents
                  for users onboarded before 2023.

                  - Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract
                  terminates at close; plan is to repoint Harbor''s transaction feed
                  at Mosaic''s engine on day 1.

                  - Marketing wants a ''Welcome'' campaign with a $50 bonus on first
                  transfer, launching close+1.

                  - Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs from
                  the last year at Harbor; nobody has read them yet.

                  - Migration moves 240k consumer users and 12k business accounts
                  into Mosaic Relay''s app on day 1 post-close, with one unified account
                  and balance.

                  - Plan is no re-verification of Harbor''s existing KYC; Harbor users
                  were already KYC''d.

                  - Harbor''s KYC ran through a vendor that shut down in 2024; pass/fail
                  results exist for everyone but underlying documents are missing
                  for users onboarded before 2023.

                  - Harbor''s transaction monitoring is a third-party SaaS whose contract
                  terminates at close; plan is to repoint the transaction feed to
                  Mosaic Relay''s engine on day 1.

                  - Diligence flagged ~40 open alerts and ''a handful'' of SARs from
                  the last year at Harbor; none have been read yet.

                  - How is the Harbor Pay acquisition structured? — Asset purchase
                  (Mosaic buys Harbor''s assets)

                  - Does Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP program currently permit relying
                  on another institution''s prior KYC without re-verification, or
                  is re-verification required? — Not sure / need to check with compliance

                  - What is known about Harbor''s ~40 open alerts and the SARs from
                  the last year? — Nothing reviewed yet — still in diligence

                  - For the four new markets opened by the combined footprint, does
                  Mosaic Relay plan to operate under Harbor''s existing licenses or
                  apply for its own? — Use/assume Harbor''s licenses

                  - For the pre-2023 Harbor users with no underlying KYC documents,
                  what is the plan to satisfy Mosaic Relay''s own BSA/AML customer
                  identification and recordkeeping obligations? — It is not yet known
                  whether Mosaic Relay''s AML/CIP program permits reliance on Harbor''s
                  prior KYC; compliance must confirm.

                  - Have the ~40 open alerts and the handful of SARs from the last
                  year been reviewed, and what did they reveal? — The open alerts
                  and SAR history have not been reviewed and remain in diligence.

                  - For the four new markets opened by the combined license footprint,
                  what is the plan for state money transmission licensing or approval
                  before onboarding those customers? — Mosaic Relay currently plans
                  to use or assume Harbor''s licenses for the four new markets.


                  ## Assumptions


                  - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay''s existing money transmission licenses
                  and Harbor''s MTLs are transferable or can be maintained through
                  the acquisition without new state approval

                  - [Assumption] The KYC pass/fail results are sufficient to satisfy
                  Mosaic Relay''s own BSA/AML program obligations without the underlying
                  documents

                  - [Assumption] The transaction monitoring repoint can be completed
                  and validated before close without a monitoring gap

                  - [Assumption] Harbor Pay is a licensed money transmitter subject
                  to state MTL regimes and federal BSA/AML obligations (not yet confirmed).

                  - [Assumption] Mosaic Relay is itself a licensed money transmitter
                  in 41 states (per the request).

                  - [Assumption] The acquisition is structured as an asset or stock
                  purchase, which affects whether Harbor''s licenses and SAR/alert
                  obligations transfer (structure not yet confirmed).

                  '
